readings.c2s1:
¶
'''thickskull''' (thik′skul), ''n.'' A dull person; a blockhead.

'''thick-skulled''' (thik′skuld), ''a.'' Dull; heavy; stupid; slow to learn.

{{smaller block|This downright fighting fool, this ''thick-skulled'' hero.
{{right|''Dryden'', All for Love, iii. 1.}}}}

'''thick-stamen''' (thik′stā″men), ''n.'' See ''Pachysandra.''

'''thick-starred''' (thik′stärd), ''a.'' Strewn thickly with stars. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|In some wynters nyht whan the firmament is clere and ''thikke-sterred.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Astrolabe, ii. 23.}}}}

'''thick-tongued''' (thik′tungd), ''a.'' Having a thick tongue; specifically, in ''herpet.'', pachyglossate.

'''thick-wind''' (thik′wind), ''n.'' Impeded respiration of the horse, somewhat louder and less free than normal breathing. {{smaller|This may be due to roaring, to asthma (heaves), or to encroachment upon the lungs of a distended stomach or pregnant uterus.}}

'''thick-winded''' (thik′win″ded), ''a.'' Affected with thick-wind, as a horse.

'''thick-witted''' (thik′wit″ed), ''a.'' Dull of wit; stupid; thick-headed.

{{smaller block|A pretty face and a sweet heart . . . often overturn a ''thick-witted'' or a light-headed man.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVI. 369.}}}}

'''thicky''' (thik′i), ''a.'' [< ''thick'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Thick. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|It was neere a ''thicky'' shade,
That broad leaues of Beech had made.
{{right|''Greene'', Descrip. of the Shepherd and his Wife.}}}}

'''thider†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''thither.'' ''Chaucer.''

'''thief<sup>1</sup>''' (thēf), ''n.''; pl. ''thieves'' (thēvz). [Early mod.
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''thiefly†''' (thēf′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''theefly, theefliche, theveli, thevelich, theofliche''; < ''thief''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Like a thief; hence, stealthily; secretly.

{{smaller block|''Theuelich'' Y am had awey fro the loond of Hebrew.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Gen. xl. 15.}}
In the night ful ''theefly'' gan he stalke.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1781.}}}}

'''thief-stolen''' (thēf′stō″ln), ''a.'' Stolen by a thief or thieves. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Had I been ''thief-stol'n'',
As my two brothers, happy!
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 6. 5.}}}}

'''thief-taker''' (thēf′tā″kėr), ''n.'' One whose business it is to find and take thieves and bring them to justice; a thief-catcher.

'''thiefteously†''', ''adv.'' Same as ''theftuously''.

'''thief-tube''' (thēf′tūb), ''n.'' A sampling-tube; a tube which may be inserted in a bung-hole, and, when filled with the liquid in the cask, withdrawn with its contents by placing the thumb over the upper end.

'''thietsee''', ''n.'' See ''theetsee''.

'''thieve''' (thēv), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''thieved'', ppr. ''thieving''. [< ME. *''theven'', < AS. ''theófian'', thieve, < ''theóf'', a thief: see ''thief''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To be a thief; practise theft; steal; prey.

{{smaller block|He knows not what may ''thieve'' upon his senses,
Or what temptation may rise.
{{right|''Shirley'', Love's Cruelty, i. 1.}}
Or proul in courts of law for human prey,
In venal senate ''thieve'', or rob on broad highway.
{{right|''Thomson'', Castle of Indolence, i. 13.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To take by theft; steal.
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|My mother still
Affirms your Psyche ''thieved'' her theories.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iii.}}}}

¶
'''thieveless''' (thēv′les), ''a.'' [Cf. ''thewless.''] Cold; forbidding. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|Wi' ''thieveless'' sneer to see his modish mien,
He, down the water, gi'es him this guid-e'en.
{{right|''Burns'', Brigs of Ayr.}}}}

'''thievery''' (thēv′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''thieveries'' (-iz). [= OFries. ''deverie'' = G. ''dieberei'' = Sw. ''tjufveri'' = Dan. ''tyveri''; as ''thieve'' + ''-ery.''] 1. The act or practice of stealing; theft.

{{smaller block|Knaverie, Villanie, and ''Thieverie!'' I smell it rank, she 's stoln, she 's gone directlie. ''Brome'', Northern Lass, ii. 6.}}

{{smaller block|We owe a great deal of picturesqueness to the quarrels and ''thieveries'' of the barons of the Middle Ages.
{{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 254.}}}}

2. That which is stolen.

{{smaller block|Injurious time now with a robber's haste
Crams his rich ''thievery'' up, he knows not how.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 4. 45.}}}}

'''thieves''', ''n.'' Plural of ''thief.''

'''thievish''' (thē′vish), ''a.'' [= D. ''diefsch'' = MLG. ''dēvisch'' = G. ''diebisch''; as ''thief'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. Addicted to, concerned in, or characterized by thievery; pertaining in any manner to theft.

{{smaller block|Or with a base and boisterous sword enforce
A ''thievish'' living on the common road.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 3. 33.}}}}

{{smaller block|O ''thievish'' Night,
Why shouldst thou, but for some felonious end,
In thy dark lantern thus close up the stars?
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 195.}}}}

2. Stealthy; furtive; secret; sly.

{{smaller block|He sitteth lurking in the ''thievish'' corners of the streets.}}
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Psalter, Ps. x. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thou by thy dial's shady stealth mayst know
Time's ''thievish'' progress to eternity.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxvii.}}}}

'''thievishly''' (thē′vish-li), ''adv.'' In a thievish manner; like a thief; by theft.

'''thievishness''' (thē′vish-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being thievish. ''Bailey'', 1727.

'''thig''' (thig), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''thigged'', ppr. ''thigging.'' [< ME. ''thiggen'', < AS. ''thicgan'', ''thicgean'', take, receive, partake of, = OS. ''thiggian'', ''thiggean'' = OHG. ''dikkan'', ''thichan'', ''thiggen'', MHG. ''digen'' = Icel. ''thiggja'', get, receive, receive hospitality for a night, = Sw. ''tigga'' = Dan. ''tigge'', beg as a mendicant. The E. form and sense are due rather to Scand. The reg. form from AS. ''thicgan'' would be ''*thidge''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To beseech; supplicate; implore; especially, to ask as alms; beg. Compare ''thigger.''

{{smaller block|And now me bus, as a beggar, my bred for to ''thigge''
At dores vpon dayes, that dayres me full sore.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 13549.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To make supplication; specifically, to profit by or live on the gifts of others; take alms. See the quotation under ''sorn.''

{{smaller block|They were fain to ''thigg'' and cry for peace and good-will.
{{right|''Pitscottie'', p. 56. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

[Prov. Eng. and Scotch in both uses.]

'''thigger''' (thig′ėr), ''n.'' [Also Sc. ''thiggar'', Shetland ''tiggar''; = Sw. ''tiggare'' = Dan. ''tigger'', a beggar; as ''thig'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who thigs; a beg-

{{RunningHeader|thick-lipped|6289|thigger}}'''thick-lipped''' (thik′lipt), ''a.'' Having thick lips, as a negro; labroid, as a fish; thickened around the edges, as an ulcer.—'''Thick-lipped perch.''' See ''perch''1. '''thicklips''' (thik′lips), ''n.'' A person having thick lips—a characteristic of the negro race: used opprobriously. {{smaller block|What a full fortune does the ''thick-lips'' owe,
If he can carry 't thus! {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 1. 66.}}}} '''thickly''' (thik′li), ''adv.'' In a thick manner, in any sense of the word ''thick;'' densely; closely; deeply; abundantly; frequently. '''thickness''' (thik′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thiknesse'', < AS. ''thicnes'', < ''thicce'', thick: see ''thick''.] 1. The state or property of being thick, in any sense; specifically, that dimension of a solid body which is at right angles both to its length and to its breadth; the third or least dimension of a solid. {{smaller block|Sex fyngre thicke a floore thereof thou pave
With lyme and asshes mixt with cole and sande,
A flake above in ''thiknesse'' of thyne hande. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 13.}}}} {{smaller block|The height of one pillar was eighteen cubits; . . . and the ''thickness'' thereof was four fingers. {{right|Jer. lii. 21.}}}} 2. That which is thick; the thick of anything; the dense, heavy, deep, or solid part. {{smaller block|The chambers were in the ''thickness'' of the wall of the court toward the east. {{right|Ezek. xlii. 10.}}}} {{smaller block|This enormous ''thickness'' of nearly three miles of Old Red Sandstone. {{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Cosmology, p. 270.}}}} 3. A fold, layer, or sheet, as of cloth or paper.—4. In ''founding'', the sand or loam placed temporarily in a mold while it is being prepared for casting. It is afterward removed, and its place is filled with the molten metal. '''thickness''' (thik′nes), ''v. t.'' [< ''thickness'', ''n.''] To reduce to a uniform thickness before dressing to shape: said of boards and timber. [Trade use.] '''thick-pleached''' (thik′plēcht), ''a.'' Thickly interwoven. {{smaller block|The prince and Count Claudio, walking in a ''thick-pleached'' alley in my orchard, were thus much overheard by a man of mine. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, i. 2. 10.}}}} '''thick-set''' (thik′set), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' 1. Set, growing, or occurring closely together; dense; luxuriant. {{smaller block|His eyeballs glare with fire, suffus'd with blood; His neck shoots up a ''thick set'' thorny wood. {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid's Metamorph., viii., Meleager and [Atalanta, l. 23.}}}} {{smaller block|Live long, ere from thy topmost head The ''thick-set'' hazel dies. {{right|''Tennyson'', Will Waterproof.}}}} 2. Thickly studded; abounding; plentifully supplied. {{smaller block|With windows of this kind the town of Curzola is ''thick-set'' in every quarter. {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 214.}}}} 3. Heavily or solidly built; stout; especially, short and stout. {{smaller block|At Grantham, I believe, he sat up all night to avoid sleeping in the next room to a ''thick-set'' squinting fellow, in a black wig and a tarnished gold-laced waistcoat. {{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, iii.}}}} {{smaller block|Laying a short, ''thickset'' finger upon my arm, he looked up in my face with an investigating air. {{right|''Bulwer'', Pelham, xxxvi.}}}} {{smaller block|'''Thick-set cord''', a kind of thick-set of which the surface is ribbed like that of corduroy.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A close or thick hedge.—'''2.''' Very thick or dense underwood; bush; scrub.—'''3.''' A kind of fustian having a nap like that of velveteen. It is used for clothes by persons engaged in manual work. '''thick-sighted''' (thik′sī″ted), ''a.'' Dim of sight; weak-sighted. {{smaller block|Whereas before she could see some furniture in her house, now she could perceive none; she was erst ''thick-sighted'', but now purblind. {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 388.}}}} '''thickskin''' (thik′skin), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' One who has a thick skin—that is, one who is insensible to or not easily irritated by taunts, reproaches, ridicule, or the like; a rude, unimpressible person. {{smaller block|The shallowest ''thick-skin'' of that barren sort. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 13.}}}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Same as ''thick-skinned.'' {{smaller block|Nor can I bide to pen some hungry scene
For ''thick-skin'' ears, and undiscerning eyne. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, i. 8.}}}} '''thick-skinned''' (thik′skind), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having a thick skin or rind: as, a ''thick-skinned'' animal; a ''thick-skinned'' orange.—'''2.''' Specifically, in ''zoöl.'', pachydermatous, as a rhinoceros; belonging to the ''Pachydermata.''—'''3.''' Insensible to reproach, ridicule, or insult; dull; stolid. {{smaller block|He is too ''thick-skinned'' to mind eloquent and indignant criticism. {{right|''The American'', IX. 387.}}}} 395 '''thickskull''' (thik′skul), ''n.''
